hbm.competition.entryBarrier.why: The only contender — China's CXMT — is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and realistically will not reach volume before 2028 — and then mostly for China's domestic market.
hbm.competition.players.0.note: Its share only falls because the market is growing: in money terms the business doubled in a year. ~90% of sales go to Nvidia: a strength and a risk at once.

hbm.competition.players.2.note: Missed an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). Coming back: lead supplier to AMD and >60% of the memory for Google's chips.
hbm.competition.players.2.tech: Spent eighteen months failing Nvidia qualification
hbm.competition.switchingCost: To change memory supplier, a customer must pass qualification again — anywhere from several months to eighteen. Until it is passed, no amount of announced capacity earns a dollar. That is why shares move slowly and predictably.
hbm.competition.takeaway: Three split the market, no one can enter, and customers cannot leave quickly — that set-up is what holds prices up. Only one thing to watch: how Nvidia divides its orders among the three at each new generation.
hbm.demand.backlog: SK Hynix holds more orders than it can produce in three years. Micron has ~$100B of contracted future revenue — several years of its revenue.
hbm.demand.contractStructure: Micron: 16 strategic agreements, ~$100B of contracted future revenue, many at a fixed price or with a floor. ~$22B of customer prepayments. Cloud giants sign multi-year contracts with a guaranteed minimum price. A letter of intent with OpenAI (Oct 2025). This is the main evidence that HBM has partly decoupled from the classic memory cycle.
hbm.demand.customerConcentration: Nvidia is ~90% of SK Hynix's sales and the industry's largest buyer. Google is scaling fastest; Amazon and Meta are more cautious. A single Nvidia allocation decision moves all three makers' shares.
hbm.demand.pricing: 2026: HBM3E up ~20% on 2025. For 2027 the makers assume a several-fold price increase. The turning point: in Q1'26 ordinary server memory (DDR5) became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a strong argument for raising HBM prices further.
hbm.demand.soldOut.0.note: all three; Micron covers ~60% of demand
hbm.demand.takeaway: Memory has never had this kind of revenue visibility: years ahead are contracted and prepaid. While the contracts hold, profits are more reliable than the market's habit from past cycles assumes — which is exactly why drawdowns like July's offer an entry point.
hbm.dependencies.correlation: HBM demand tracks hyperscaler budget announcements with a 2–3 quarter lag — their quarterly results work as a free leading indicator.
hbm.dependencies.downstream: Buyers: Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Their 2026 data-centre budgets run $600–725B (+60–77% year on year). Microsoft named more expensive memory outright as the reason its costs rose ~$25B — HBM prices already sit inside the giants' budgets.
hbm.dependencies.takeaway: The whole chain rests on 3–4 irreplaceable suppliers: Namics (private), Hanmi, TSMC, Ibiden. Two implications: this key constraint can be bought directly (Hanmi, Besi, Ibiden) — and a failure at any one of them stops all three makers.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.0.item: The special adhesive for memory assembly
hbm.dependencies.upstream.0.note: The sole supplier to SK Hynix. The shares cannot be bought, but that exclusivity is exactly why competitors cannot replicate the industry's best assembly method.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.1.item: The machines that bond the memory layers
hbm.dependencies.upstream.1.note: ~71% of the world market. The cleanest listed way to buy this key memory-assembly constraint.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.2.item: Solderless bonding machines (the assembly of the future)
hbm.dependencies.upstream.2.note: Needed once chips go above 16 layers (~2029). Already selected by Micron.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.3.item: The substrate board under the chip
hbm.dependencies.upstream.3.note: ~35% of the market. Every new multi-layer chip needs more substrate layers — demand grows faster than the chip market itself.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.4.note: Nearly 100% of AI-class assembly of this kind. Without a slot in its queue a finished accelerator cannot be produced — a mandatory link.
hbm.dependencies.upstream.5.item: The machines that drill the channels through the chip
hbm.dependencies.upstream.5.note: A duopoly. But memory is a small part of their vast business, so the exposure is diluted.
hbm.expectations.impliedGrowth: SK Hynix trades at ~5–8x forward earnings, Micron at ~12x — on record margins (SK Hynix's operating margin is 72%). That combination says outright: the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth. This is classic cycle-peak pricing, not the valuation of a growing business.
hbm.expectations.marketBelieves: The market treats 2026–2027 as peak profit and compresses the multiple in advance — in July 2026 the shares fell >20% on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.

hbm.expectations.takeaway: HBM is priced as a peak cyclical asset: a low forward P/E is a warning, not an invitation. The anomaly is that contracts and Nvidia qualification could, for the first time, stretch the peak beyond past cycles. If so, the market is wrong on the downside; if not, the low multiple honestly reflects a near turn in 2028.
hbm.expectations.verdict: SK Hynix is cheap if the shortage holds through 2027; otherwise fair
hbm.expectations.weThink: HBM has partly decoupled from the commodity cycle for the first time — floor-priced contracts, ~$22B of prepayments and the Nvidia qualification barrier stretch the peak out. If SK Hynix's chief is right that the shortage runs past 2030, then ~5–8x forward is far too cheap. The disagreement is not about direction but duration: the market looks at a quarter, we look at two contract cycles.
hbm.intro:
HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) is memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin DRAM dies and mounted on a shared substrate right up against the processor. The binding constraint on a large AI model is not arithmetic speed but the rate at which data arrives: ordinary memory hangs off a narrow bus, centimetres of board traces away, and the processor idles waiting. HBM removes that constraint — data travels over thousands of parallel lines across millimetres, and a single stack delivers more than a terabyte per second. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without HBM.

How it works. Ordinary DRAM dies are first thinned for this: the wafer is ground from the back from roughly 780 down to 30–50 microns, or a tall stack will not fit the package height and will shed heat badly. Thousands of micro-holes are then etched all the way through each thinned die and filled with copper — these are the through-silicon vias (TSVs), vertical wires connecting every layer at once. Then 8, 12 or 16 dies are stacked and bonded: either through micro solder bumps between layers (thermocompression), or, from 16-layer HBM4 onward, copper directly to copper with no gap (hybrid bonding). The stack sits on top of a bottom logic die (the base die), which runs the whole memory and talks to the processor. The finished stack is mounted on a silicon interposer beside the processor, putting memory and processor in one package.

The hard, expensive part here is not the memory cells but assembling the stack without defects and getting the heat out. At 12–16 layers with thousands of connections, one bad die or one unbonded joint kills the entire stack, taking every good layer beneath it with it. The taller the stack, the more tightly hot dies are packed and the harder it is to pull heat out of the middle, so thinning and the bonding method decide directly how many stacks come out good. The spread in stack yield is the main hidden profit lever: Samsung's HBM4 memory yielded only around 50% in early 2026 (nearly every second die scrapped), whereas the leader's proven bonding process loses markedly less. Whoever assembles with fewer defects takes the margin.

Who pays, and how much. HBM is the most expensive part of an accelerator: a single chip carries 6–8 stacks, and memory accounts for roughly 63% of the cost of a finished AI chip, against only ~13% for the compute die itself (Epoch AI). One HBM4 stack costs ~$500–550, meaning $3–4K of memory in every accelerator; each generation costs more — from ~$200 (HBM3) to $300 (HBM3E) and $500+ (HBM4). Buyers pay without haggling, because without HBM the accelerator simply does not work and the delivery queue is booked years out: cloud giants and accelerator makers prepay to reserve capacity — Micron alone holds ~$22B of customer prepayments and ~$100B of contracted future revenue. The makers, in turn, are putting tens of billions into expansion: SK Hynix has up to $75B of capex through 2028, roughly 80% of it in HBM.

Three makers hold the market: SK Hynix ~56%, Samsung and Micron at roughly ~21% each. The segment itself grows from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028) on Micron's estimate — faster than any other part of memory; demand added +130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026.

One term that recurs below: a «node» (process technology), such as 3 nm or 2 nm, is a generation of chip manufacturing technology. The nanometre figure is a nominal label for transistor size: the smaller it is, the finer and denser the transistors and the faster and more efficient the chip — but the harder and costlier the node is to master. Only TSMC, Samsung and Intel can run leading-edge nodes (3 nm and below); «mature» nodes (28–45 nm and older) are commodity technology, cheap and widely available.
hbm.marketSizing.bomShare.note: of an AI chip's cost is memory (two years ago it was 52%); the compute die itself is only ~13%. Buying «Nvidia's suppliers», an investor is in fact buying memory suppliers.
hbm.marketSizing.takeaway: The market triples by 2028 (~$35B → ~$100B), and it is paid for by the data centres of giants who have the money. The direct beneficiaries are the three makers: SK Hynix (KRX: 000660), Micron (NASDAQ: MU), Samsung (KRX: 005930).
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.mix: From 2027 growth rests more on price than on volume. Excellent for profit, but price is the most fragile support: it breaks first when supply catches demand.
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.price: 2026 contracts were signed ~20% higher; for 2027 the makers assume a several-fold price increase. Price-led growth is the most profitable kind: it falls almost entirely to the margins of SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron.
hbm.marketSizing.volumeVsPrice.volume: Demand grew 130% in 2025 and another ~70% in 2026. The fastest growth is in the giants' custom chips (Google, Amazon): they need 80% more HBM in 2026 against +23% for ordinary GPUs — demand no longer rests on Nvidia alone.

hbm.mentalModel.drivers.2.note: a single Nvidia allocation decision moves all three makers' shares: SK Hynix holds ~70% of HBM4 for Vera Rubin, but failing qualification on a new generation cost Samsung the whole Blackwell cycle.
hbm.mentalModel.framework: The companies called «Nvidia's suppliers» earn primarily on memory: HBM is up to 63% of an AI chip's cost, and only three makers can assemble it. Until new capacity arrives (expected by 2028), demand exceeds supply and gross margins reach ~72%. Profits hold while the shortage holds; once capacity catches demand, the cycle turns — that is memory's industry pattern.
hbm.mentalModel.revenueFormula: Revenue = number of Nvidia/AMD accelerators × HBM per accelerator (6–8 chips) × price per chip (rising each generation) × market share
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.0.note: changing supplier or generation means re-qualifying at the customer, anywhere from several months to eighteen; until that is done, announced capacity earns nothing. Missing qualification on HBM3E cost Samsung an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell).
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.1.note: SK Hynix bonds layers with ~20% less scrap and better heat removal, thanks to its proprietary method using Namics' exclusive adhesive. Whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin; the taller the stack, the more that gap matters.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.2.note: SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%; entry is closed — CXMT is 3 generations (6–8 years) behind and cut off from equipment. But with HBM4 all three passed qualification for the first time — that is competition inside a generation, not an SK Hynix monopoly.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.3.note: $75B of investment at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. That capital threshold shuts newcomers out, but it also becomes a risk for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.4.note: Micron holds ~$100B of contracted future revenue and ~$22B of prepayments, many contracts with a price floor. For the first time memory is partly decoupling from the commodity cycle — but 2028 coverage is still only ~40%.
hbm.moatBreakdown.components.5.note: this is still memory: the product standardises from generation to generation, and in 2027–2028 new fabs from all three plus CXMT arrive at once. In July 2026 the sector already fell >20% on the fear of a turn alone.
hbm.moatBreakdown.takeaway: The protection is real, but this is not subscription software — it is memory. It rests on a combination: Nvidia qualification + defect-free bonding technology + the capital threshold. The one unassailable part is the difficulty of assembling without scrap, where SK Hynix leads. All of it weakens as generations standardise and new capacity arrives by 2028 — hence an honest three for commoditisation.

hbm.problems.items.0.gap: To enter, a supplier must pass Nvidia's qualification from scratch — anywhere from several months to eighteen; Samsung failed it on HBM3E (the previous stacked-memory generation) and lost an entire chip generation (Blackwell, 2024). The only new contender, China's CXMT, is three generations behind (~6–8 years), cut off from key equipment by US export controls, and will realistically not reach volume before 2028 — mostly for its domestic market. A new memory fab takes 18–36 months, with output no earlier than 2028.
hbm.problems.items.0.problem: HBM output is capped not by the memory wafers themselves but by two final-assembly steps, and both are sold out. First, building a stack of 12–16 dies with thousands of vertical connections through the silicon (TSVs — vertical channels through silicon) at a low scrap rate. Second, mounting the finished stack on a silicon substrate right against the processor (CoWoS packaging — chip and memory on one substrate; only TSMC does it). From the HBM4 generation, the bottom logic die of the chip also goes to TSMC. A single accelerator carries 6–8 stacks worth $3–4K, HBM already takes 22–30% of the whole industry's wafers, 2026 memory is fully sold out and ~90% of 2027 is contracted.
hbm.problems.items.0.solution: This can only be relieved through higher stack yield and assembly throughput, not through new wafer fabs. SK Hynix is first to perfect the layer-bonding process for each generation (for 16-layer HBM4 the industry moves to hybrid bonding — welding dies copper to copper with no gap). TSMC is expanding CoWoS packaging capacity (chip and memory on one substrate) and taking on the HBM4 base die. In parallel, the scarcest link of all is the queue for assembly machines: they are made by Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI), and they are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.problems.items.0.winners: SK Hynix (KRX: 000660) — 56.4% of the market, first to pass qualification each generation, with ~70% of HBM4 memory reserved for Nvidia's new Vera Rubin accelerators; it wins on the best stack yield. TSMC (NYSE: TSM) — holds CoWoS packaging and, from HBM4, makes the logic die, so the next scarce link moves directly to it. Plus Hanmi and Besi: all three makers buy their assembly machines.
hbm.problems.takeaway: Relieving this constraint strengthens the current leaders: what is scarce is precisely SK Hynix's stack yield and TSMC's CoWoS packaging — the things a newcomer cannot replicate. It does not open the door to a new player.
hbm.risks.0.note: Memory is close to an exchange-traded commodity: the three makers' product is similar and they expand fabs in the same years, so supply regularly overshoots demand and prices collapse. Past collapses: 2018–19 (Micron −56%), 2022–23 (−50%, SK Hynix loss-making). HBM is partly protected by multi-year contracts, but not fully — the sector already fell >20% in July 2026.
hbm.risks.1.note: The US ban (Dec 2024) on shipping HBM and equipment to China. Short-term it supports prices; the long-term risk is China building its own (CXMT).
hbm.risks.2.note: Practically ruled out: a memory fab is $30–50B and 7–10 years. Custom HBM versions only deepen customer dependence.
hbm.risks.3.note: The risk window is 2027–2028, when all three plus CXMT add capacity at the same time.
hbm.risks.4.note: SK Hynix depends on Nvidia for ~90%; any shift to multi-sourcing redistributes shares sharply.
hbm.risks.5.note: Failing qualification on a new generation is a real risk: Samsung's miss on HBM3E cost it an entire Nvidia chip generation (Blackwell).
hbm.roadmap.disruption.0.angle: Not a threat but a new market: it is being developed by the HBM leader itself (SK Hynix) together with SanDisk. It hits ordinary SSDs, not HBM. The way to play it is SanDisk (NASDAQ: SNDK) and SK Hynix (KRX: 000660).
hbm.roadmap.disruption.0.detail: This is flash memory (as in an ordinary SSD), but stacked in layers and connected almost as close to the processor as HBM. It gives 8–16x the capacity and reads almost as fast, but writes slowly — so it suits holding an already-trained model rather than training one. First inference hardware: early 2027.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.angle: Complements HBM rather than competing with it. Volume production is Micron's (NASDAQ: MU) — the same winner as in HBM: for it this is one more growing product.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.1.detail: Modules of familiar memory (the same kind as in smartphones), but placed right against the processor. They give large capacity markedly cheaper than HBM, but several times slower. Their job is to hold what does not fit in HBM and relieve it on capacity.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.angle: Does not affect the decision on a 2-year horizon. It is being developed by the same Samsung and SK Hynix — for them a far-off option, not a risk of losing the market.
hbm.roadmap.disruption.2.detail: The idea of building simple computation into the memory chip itself, to move data to the processor less often and save energy. Technically elegant, but the timelines keep slipping by years, the software does not exist, and it is not deployed in real data centres yet.
hbm.roadmap.generations.0.note: The first volume generation (Nvidia H100); SK Hynix took nearly all of it.
hbm.roadmap.generations.1.note: Nvidia's Blackwell chip generation (2024). Samsung failed qualification and missed the cycle — a lesson in how share is lost here.
hbm.roadmap.generations.2.note: For Nvidia's new accelerators (Rubin) and AMD's (MI400). All three passed qualification for the first time — competition inside a generation.
hbm.roadmap.generations.2.spec: channel twice as wide; up to 2 TB/s
hbm.roadmap.generations.3.note: Memory turns from a commodity into a made-to-order product — the makers' margin rises further.
hbm.roadmap.generations.4.note: The harder the technology, the harder it is for new players to catch up — the leaders' protection only strengthens.
hbm.roadmap.takeaway: There is no replacement for HBM on a 2026–2028 horizon: every «competitor» either complements it or was created by the HBM makers themselves. The real technology risk is one maker failing qualification on a new generation (Samsung already lost a whole cycle that way).

hbm.scenarios.takeaway: The best set-up in all of memory, but not an endless one: the base case gives a solid ~15% while the shortage holds, and the bear case is gentler than in ordinary memory — contracts and prepayments prop up the floor. The decision turns on one thing: getting out before the 2028 turn rather than sitting through it.

hbm.supply.capacityAdds.0.detail: Building the largest new memory campus at ~$89B — but meaningful output from it only arrives around 2030.
hbm.supply.capacityAdds.1.detail: Expanding fabs for HBM: the target is roughly double the output by end-2026, with new buildings only coming online in 2028.
hbm.supply.capacityAdds.2.detail: Building new fabs in the US and Singapore, ~$20B invested in a year; meaningful output only from 2027–2028.
hbm.supply.crowdingOut: Every wafer used for HBM yields a third as many gigabytes as one used for ordinary memory, and HBM already takes 22–30% of the industry's wafers. That pushes up the price of all other memory too (+90% in a quarter) — the same three makers earn twice.
hbm.supply.leadTime: A new memory fab takes 18–36 months from decision to product. Everything started now yields output no earlier than 2028: the shortage physically cannot be relieved before then.
hbm.supply.takeaway: The shortage is guaranteed through 2027 — that is what the whole thesis rests on. The dangerous window is 2028: new fabs from all three plus CXMT arrive at once. The exit signal is spot prices turning down and sector analysts using the words «market correction».
hbm.supply.utilization: Memory fabs are running flat out: every production line inside the fabs is fully loaded, none idle. So output cannot be added quickly without building new fabs.
hbm.thesis.bigIdea: The market prices HBM as ordinary cyclical memory about to collapse. But HBM has quietly decoupled from the commodity cycle: it is sold out years ahead on prepaid contracts with price floors, and its real constraint is not wafers but defect-free assembly yield. So both the high price and the record margin last longer than the market assumes — and the yield leader (SK Hynix) keeps extending its lead.
hbm.thesis.stream.0.t: Where the money in an AI chip actually sits
hbm.thesis.stream.1.t: An investor buying «Nvidia's suppliers» thinks they are buying compute. In fact they are buying memory. In the cost of a modern AI chip, 63% is HBM memory and only about 13% is the compute die itself. Over the past two years the value quietly moved from logic to memory: every accelerator carries 6–8 HBM modules worth $3–4K — more than the processor.

hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.2.label: Samsung — coming back
hbm.thesis.stream.20.items.2.note: missed an Nvidia generation (Blackwell); recovering through AMD and Google
hbm.thesis.stream.21.t: What is already priced in — and where the anomaly is
hbm.thesis.stream.22.t: And here is the anomaly. A record 72% operating margin, years of prepaid backlog — and SK Hynix trades at 5–8x earnings, Micron at about 12x. A low multiple on a record margin is not cheapness, it is the market betting on an imminent profit fall. The market is pricing a cycle peak, not a growing business.
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.0.n: memory at a peak usually trades at 8–12x — this is cheaper still
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.1.n: the cheapest way in, and the only way to buy HBM on a US exchange
hbm.thesis.stream.23.items.2.n: a record — and precisely what the market thinks cannot hold
hbm.thesis.stream.24.t: Our read: the argument is not about direction but about duration. Contract price floors, $22B of prepayments and the barrier of Nvidia qualification stretch the peak out. If the shortage holds through 2027 (and SK Hynix's chief says beyond 2030), then 5–8x is far too cheap. The market is looking at a quarter; we are looking at two contract cycles.
hbm.thesis.stream.26.t: The thesis rests on the shortage. Three signals would say it is over — and it is worth remembering that from 2027 growth rests increasingly on price, and price is the first thing to break when supply catches up:
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.0.1: Share redistribution and a price war — the leader's margin compresses
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.0: New fabs from all three + China's CXMT passes qualification (2028)
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.1.1: Supply catches demand — the shortage ends
hbm.thesis.stream.27.rows.2.1: The price floor the thesis stands on stops holding
hbm.thesis.stream.28.t: None of them is lit yet: contracts keep reaching further out, and Samsung has not closed the yield gap.
hbm.thesis.stream.29.t: The bottom line — if you remember one thing
hbm.thesis.stream.3.t: What HBM is, and why nothing works without it
hbm.thesis.stream.30.t: HBM triples to ~$100B by 2028, and it is paid for by the data centres of giants who have the money. Memory has quietly become the most expensive and the most heavily contracted part of an AI chip — and the market still prices it as a commodity on the edge of a crash.
hbm.thesis.stream.31.t: Compressed into one thought: the market is pricing a collapse, and the contracts say otherwise. The best-protected ways to buy it are the yield leader (SK Hynix) and the only maker available on a US exchange (Micron), for as long as the shortage holds, plus the bonding machines (Hanmi/Besi), which are needed however the shares fall. Samsung is a separate bet on a comeback and a share shift.
hbm.thesis.stream.4.t: HBM is several ordinary memory dies stacked on top of one another and threaded with vertical channels through the silicon (TSVs), so data travels up and down rather than around. The finished stack sits right against the compute chip on a shared substrate. Without it the accelerator «starves»: the compute core idles waiting for data. Each generation costs more than the last: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.thesis.stream.5.t: What the market thinks: «it's memory, it will crash»
hbm.thesis.stream.6.t: Memory has always been a brutal commodity cycle: boom → fab build-out → glut → price collapse. The market prices HBM by the same reflex. In July 2026 the makers' shares fell more than 20% — on record results. Everyone knows memory is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first.
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.l: earnings is what SK Hynix costs
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.0.n: on a record 72% operating margin — the market is pricing a profit fall, not growth
hbm.thesis.stream.7.items.1.n: on a record quarter — the classic «this is the cycle peak» reaction
hbm.thesis.stream.8.t: Why HBM decoupled from the cycle
hbm.thesis.stream.9.t: But HBM is not traded on an exchange at a spot price the way ordinary memory is. It is contracted years ahead, prepaid, with a price floor, and co-designed with the customer. Commodities do not behave like that.
hbm.tldr.0: The best supply/demand set-up memory has seen in 40 years: three makers share the market (SK Hynix 56%, Samsung ~21%, Micron ~21%), all of 2026 is sold out, and the market goes from ~$35B (2025) to ~$100B (2028), growing ~40% a year.
hbm.tldr.1: The best return-for-risk is SK Hynix (the leader: ~70% of HBM4 supply — the newest generation of this stacked memory — is reserved for Vera Rubin, Nvidia's next accelerator generation, on a 72% operating margin). Micron is the cheapest way in (forward P/E ~12). Hanmi / Besi / TSMC supply the equipment and the final assembly for this link.
hbm.tldr.2: The main risk is cyclicality: memory gets cheaper the moment supply catches demand, and by 2027–2028 all three makers will have finished new fabs. The sector already fell >20% in July 2026. The question is whether multi-year contracts and prepayments hold the price when that new supply arrives.
hbm.unitEconomics.costCurve: SK Hynix produces at the lowest cost and with the least scrap, thanks to its proprietary layer-bonding method: on average ~20% less scrap and better heat removal than the method its competitors at Samsung and Micron use.
hbm.unitEconomics.grossMargin: HBM costs 5–6x more than ordinary memory per gigabyte. The 2026 paradox: ordinary server memory rose so far that it became more profitable per wafer than HBM — a sure sign HBM prices will be raised in 2027.
hbm.unitEconomics.pricePerUnit: One multi-layer HBM4 chip costs ~$500–550, and an accelerator carries 6–8 of them (i.e. $3–4K of memory in every chip). Each generation costs more: $200 (HBM3) → $300 (HBM3E) → $500+ (HBM4).
hbm.unitEconomics.takeaway: The share of chips assembled defect-free is the main hidden profit lever: whoever assembles with less scrap takes the margin. Today that is SK Hynix. The main share-shift scenario is a Samsung breakthrough on scrap; watch its quarterly margin for it.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.0.label: Samsung — HBM4 memory
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.0.value: ~50% defect-free (Jan 2026) → ~60% (mid-2026). Nearly every second die is scrapped — which is why Samsung trails on margin.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.1.label: Samsung — new bonding (hybrid bonding)
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.1.value: ~10% defect-free on prototypes — the future technology is not yet ready to sell.
hbm.unitEconomics.yields.2.value: the figures are not disclosed, but SK Hynix runs a proven combination (mature memory + a TSMC base die) — lower scrap risk.
hbm.universe.0.note: The leader at 56%; +571% over 52 weeks. The most confident single bet in this link.
hbm.universe.1.note: The cheapest way in; ~$100B of future revenue contracted. Reports 22 Sep 2026.
hbm.universe.2.note: The purest picks and shovels: layer-bonding machines, ~71% of the market; qualified for HBM4.
hbm.universe.3.note: Micron's TCB vendor for HBM4; the hybrid-bonding leader for 16-hi and above.
hbm.universe.4.note: ~100% of AI-class CoWoS; foundry for the HBM4 base die.
hbm.universe.5.exposure: memory is one part of the conglomerate
hbm.universe.5.note: Recovering in HBM; turnkey HBM4 (its own foundry).
hbm.universe.6.note: Less re-rated; each chip needs ever more substrate layers.
hbm.update.bottomLine: Not nothing, but not a break either: Hynix's profit was trimmed slightly, efficiency is real, China is coming, capacity is being built — but demand has not broken. What the market re-rated is less the profit than the duration: investors are no longer willing to pay years ahead for peak margins (everyone knows the sector is cyclical, and everyone rushes to price the peak first). Only facts will settle the argument — durable orders, prices that hold, and profit. The nearest clean demand signal is TSMC's report; Hynix reports in about two weeks, into an already lowered bar.
hbm.update.headline: Is July's memory panic worth believing?
hbm.update.stories.0.detail: Hynix's Q2 profit guidance came in ~8% below expectations, and 2026–27 estimates were cut 9–11%. But the cause is company-specific: Hynix has more HBM in its revenue mix, and HBM under long contracts rises in price more slowly than ordinary memory, so its average selling price lagged the market. Meanwhile the margin is a record (~75%), profit is up 500% year on year, and by Q3 pricing catches up with the market as HBM4 ships. This is a Hynix quirk, not weak demand.
hbm.update.stories.0.title: SK Hynix's «miss»
hbm.update.stories.1.detail: Nvidia's platforms (Grace Blackwell and the coming Vera Rubin) face a direct competitor for the first time: AMD's Helios rack bets on an HBM4 memory advantage, and Microsoft has joined the project. For the memory makers this is a second large accelerator buyer besides Nvidia — HBM demand stops resting on a single customer and becomes more durable.
hbm.update.stories.1.title: AMD's Helios rack challenges Nvidia through HBM4; Microsoft is a new customer
hbm.update.stories.1.verdict: HBM demand extends beyond Nvidia — a plus for the three
hbm.update.stories.2.detail: Hynix's record $26.5B equity raise pulled in a lot of memory-dedicated capital, leveraged Korean funds amplified the move, and geopolitics added to it. Tellingly, the biggest fallers were the NAND names — the ones least connected to Hynix's issue, to efficiency, or to HBM supply. This looks like an overcrowded position unwinding, not demand breaking.
hbm.update.stories.2.title: The share-price fall itself
hbm.update.stories.3.detail: A startup compressed a model from ~54 to ~3.9 GB — impressive. But in practice it still needs ~9.4 GB of memory (with overhead), and answer quality falls. This continues a years-long compression trend rather than a sudden «HBM is no longer needed». The question is which moves faster: memory saved, or query volume. So far, the cheaper inference gets, the more inference there is. It matters over years, but it is not a reason to cut forecasts now.
hbm.update.stories.3.title: Model compression (efficiency)
hbm.update.stories.3.verdict: the trend is real, but not a collapse
hbm.update.stories.4.detail: ASML (which makes the machines for memory fabs) expects +75% memory revenue this year and +30% machine output by 2027 — the makers are genuinely investing in build-out. But upgrading existing machines adds only ~4.5% of throughput; serious growth takes new fabs, new machines and time. This is the future supply response (2027–28), not July's shock. Good for equipment demand now, but it pressures the duration of the cycle later.
hbm.update.stories.4.title: ASML's equipment signals
hbm.update.stories.4.verdict: supply is growing, but only by 2027–28
hbm.update.stories.5.detail: Two independent research teams, in Korea and Japan, showed new ways to integrate memory that route around HBM's thermal limits. As layer counts rise, pulling heat out of the stack becomes an ever more serious problem and one of the main engineering barriers for HBM4 and the generations after it. This is a question of future chip design, not of current demand.
hbm.update.stories.5.title: New memory architectures against HBM overheating
hbm.update.stories.5.verdict: heat is a growing engineering constraint, not a risk today
hbm.update.summary: Three weeks ago memory was in high demand — now it is being avoided: the leaders are down 20%+ from their late-June highs and ~$1.5T has left semiconductors, while the S&P barely moved. Below: which of July's fears actually change supply and demand, and which only explain the share prices.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNext: The binding constraint moves to TSMC's fab (NYSE: TSM): from the HBM4 generation the bottom logic die of the chip is made on its capacity, and it is that capacity (plus the defect-free share on new generations) that will be short in the next cycle.
hbm.valueCapture.bottleneckNow: Output is capped not by the wafers themselves but by final assembly of the multi-layer chip: fine-drilling the channels through the layers, the queue for bonding machines, and the share of assembled chips that come out defect-free. The money in that goes to the makers of the assembly machines — Hanmi (KRX: 042700) and Besi (AMS: BESI).
hbm.valueCapture.capitalIntensity: Growth takes enormous capital: $75B at SK Hynix alone through 2028 (~80% of it in HBM), plus an $89B new campus. Good for the equipment suppliers; risky for the makers themselves if demand wobbles.
hbm.valueCapture.takeaway: The margin sits with the memory makers (70–85%) and in the key assembly constraints. The best-protected ways to buy it: the makers themselves during the short years, plus Hanmi/Besi, whose machines are needed however the shares split among the three.
hbm.verdict.bear.0: Oversupply in 2028: the new fabs together (three makers plus China's CXMT) outrun demand growth, and analysts start talking about a «market correction».
hbm.verdict.bear.1: China (CXMT — a new Chinese memory maker) breaks the trio's market: its memory passes qualification at a Western giant, its defect-free share rises, and it completes an $8.55B IPO.
hbm.verdict.bear.2: The ordinary memory cycle returns: spot prices turn down, inventories build, and margins come off the 85–92% peak.
hbm.verdict.bull.0: The shortage holds to 2028: on the Q3–Q4 2026 calls the makers say «sold out» again, and final chip assembly at TSMC stays short.
hbm.verdict.bull.1: HBM (stacked memory) prices rise several-fold in 2027: visible in contract pricing (TrendForce data) and in the average selling prices the makers disclose in H2 2026.
hbm.verdict.bull.2: HBM profits have decoupled from the old memory cycle: contracted commitments and prepayments keep growing (~$100B at Micron), and the price floors written into contracts hold.
hbm.verdict.horizon: about 2 years — the window of HBM shortage and high prices (2026–2027); by 2027–2028 new fabs catch demand and the cycle turns down.
hbm.verdict.keyQuestion: Will HBM demand absorb the 2027–2028 fabs — or will overbuild collapse prices the way it did in 2018 and 2022?
hbm.verdict.summary: A strong structural story: memory is acutely short, only three companies make it, and demand is contracted years ahead — hence the record prices and margins. But memory carries a built-in risk: by 2027–2028 all three makers (plus the Chinese newcomer CXMT) will have finished new fabs. When that supply arrives and catches demand, memory prices fall and profits with them — that is how every previous cycle ended. Hence a 7, not a 9.
hbm.whatIsIt: Memory assembled into a vertical stack of thin dies and placed right up against the compute chip. A large AI model sits idle not for lack of arithmetic speed but because ordinary memory cannot feed it data fast enough; this stack feeds it through a far wider pipe over a very short distance. That is why an AI accelerator cannot do without it — it is the most expensive and the scarcest part of the chip.
